newsitem.title: JORDAN: King Hussein says Jordan won't revoke press law.
newsitem.headline: King Hussein says Jordan won't revoke press law.

text.p: King Hussein said on Thursday Jordan would not revoke tough restrictions on the press imposed last month despite protests from journalists and opposition groups.
"Freedom has its limits," the king told a university audience in the southern Jordanian town of Kerak.

The restrictions, unveiled three weeks ago, include tight curbs on reporting, stiffer fines for offenders and crushing financial obligations which are expected to force many of Jordan's privately owned weekly newspapers to shut down.
Opponents said the law was aimed at gagging criticism of the government before parliamentary elections due to be held in November.
Leaders of three of Jordan's influential professional unions resigned in protest and opposition groups are planning a sit-in next week.

"There has been a lot of talk these days about a ceiling on freedom. The fact is there is no ceiling...But freedom has its limits. The limits are: not encroaching on other people's freedoms; not harming the nation, or mocking national interests and unity," the king said.
He was speaking in the southern town of Kerak, rocked by rioting last August after the government cut bread subsidies. His comments were shown on television.
"The (law) was amended after study. We approved it and signed it and we will not go back on our signature and we will not go back on our decision," the king added.
The amended press law was announced just days after the king hit out at the "deteriorating morals" of journalists in Jordan.

Critics of the press restrictions say they were rushed into law in violation of the constitution while parliament was in recess. They have also attacked the government for passing a law governing the elections themselves during the recess.

Under the new press law weekly newspapers, often boisterous critics of King Hussein's 1994 peace treaty with Israel, have been given just three months to increase their capital 20-fold to 300,000 dinars from 15,000 dinars.
Few are expected to be able to meet the new requirements.

The law forbids journalists outright from writing about Jordan's armed forces and security services. It retains a ban on items which offend the king and royal family, contain contempt of religion, damage national unity, encourage crime, undermine confidence in the Jordanian dinar or offend public morals.

The prohibitions cover drawings and pictures as well as written articles. Fines for violators were raised to at least 15,000 dinars ($21,200) from 1,000 dinars. Offending newspapers can be suspended from publication.
